Surah 109: The Disbelievers (Al-Kaafiroon) was revealed at Mecca. It concerns the speaker and the disbelievers. The speaker declares that the speaker will not worship what the disbelievers worship, and that the disbelievers do not worship what the speaker worships. The unit ends by assigning the speaker's religion to the speaker and the disbelievers' religion to the disbelievers.

s: Surah 109: The Disbelievers (Al-Kaafiroon) was revealed at Mecca. It declares the separation between the speaker's worship and the disbelievers' worship, and between their religions.
The disbelievers are addressed by the speaker. They do not worship what the speaker worships, and their religion is assigned to them.

l: the speaker's religion, Surah 109: The Disbelievers (Al-Kaafiroon)

l: the speaker's object of worship, Surah 109: The Disbelievers (Al-Kaafiroon)
s: The speaker worships an object that the disbelievers do not worship.

l: the disbelievers' object of worship, Surah 109: The Disbelievers (Al-Kaafiroon)
s: The disbelievers worship an object that the speaker does not worship.

It instructs the addressed person to hymn the praises of the Lord and seek forgiveness, because He is ever ready to show mercy.

Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad) concerns Abu Lahab, his fate, and his wife. Abu Lahab’s power will perish, and he will perish. His wealth and gains will not exempt him from being plunged into flaming Fire. His wife, the wood-carrier, will have a halter of palm-fibre upon her neck.

l: Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad), Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad)
s: It concerns the perishing of Abu Lahab, the failure of his wealth and gains to exempt him, and the punishment of him and his wife.

l: Abu Lahab, Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad)

l: wife (Abu Lahab's wife), Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad)

l: fire (Abu Lahab's punishment), Surah 111: The Palm Fibre (Al-Masad)

Surah 112, titled Sincerity (Al-Ikhlaas), was revealed at Mecca. It instructs the reader to say that Allah is One and eternally Besought of all. It states that Allah neither begets nor was begotten, and that none is comparable unto Him.
Surah 112 is titled Sincerity (Al-Ikhlaas) and was revealed at Mecca. It teaches that Allah is One, eternally Besought of all, neither begets nor was begotten, and has none comparable unto Him.

Surah 113: The Dawn (Al-Falaq) was revealed at Mecca. It tells the listener to seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak. It names evil from created things, intense darkness, malignant witchcraft, and the envier when he envies. The passage concerns protection from these forms of evil.

Surah 114: Mankind (An-Naas) was revealed at Mecca. It tells mankind to seek refuge from the evil of the sneaking whisperer.

l: The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: The document presents religious teachings on government, daily conduct, death, and destiny. Rulers, described as God’s shadows on earth, are accountable to God for justice, while leaders, men, wives, and slaves each bear duties; oppression is strongly condemned. It urges lawful obedience and control of anger. It then teaches proper belief and conduct: compassion, learning, medicine, deliberation, family and neighborly care, and avoidance of false dreams, spying, excess praise, and worldly distractions. Finally, it describes the souls of believers and unbelievers after death, treatment of the dead, resurrection, Paradise, Hell Fire, and God’s determination and guidance alongside human responsibility for works.

l: Government, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Government is a trust from God; its holder will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection unless worthy, just, and good.

l: God, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: God creates medicine, Paradise, and Hell Fire; determines every created thing; turns hearts; writes each person’s place in fire or Paradise; forgives, rewards, punishes, and appoints punishment for picture-making. God’s favour and mercy govern entry into Paradise, while pursuit of knowledge is directed toward it. God’s pleasure follows a father’s pleasure and displeasure follows a father’s displeasure, and loving-kindness depends on love for God’s creatures and children. God also makes government a subject of inquiry and forbids Paradise to an oppressive prince.

l: Day of Resurrection, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_a time of punishment [for those who draw pictures] On the Day of Resurrection, wealth for which charity was not given becomes a serpent that attacks its possessor. Liars and those who neglected the Korān are punished until that day, and signs preceding it include the loss of knowledge, ignorance, wickedness, drinking liquor, fewer men, and many women.

l: king, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: King, called God’s shadow upon the earth, receives rewards and subjects’ gratitude when just, but bears sin when he oppresses.

l: subject, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: A group owed justice and good conduct turns to the king when oppressed, yet is instructed to obey rulers submissively.

l: leader, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: A government leader serves as the subject’s guardian and will be asked about that subject.

l: slave, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: A slave is portrayed as a shepherd responsible for a master’s property, accountable for its care, and entitled to obedience when appointed to rule, regardless of appearance.

l: Paradise, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_surrounded_by distress and troubles [to test those who seek it] Paradise is created by God and initially appears so desirable that Gabriel expects everyone who hears of it to seek it. God surrounds it with distress and troubles, and the Prophet’s vision includes a house for martyrs and a dwelling prepared for him.

l: prince, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_forbidden Paradise [if he oppresses the subject and dies] A prince who oppresses his subject and dies is denied Paradise by God.

l: Prophet of God, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: The Prophet of God gives authoritative religious orders and worldly guidance as a man among men. He commands obedience to just, good princes even when they withhold rights; teaches respect for any bier; and addresses death, graves, consolation, duty, punishment, reward, and entry into Paradise through God’s mercy.

l: obedience, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Obedience is due to lawful commands, but not to sinful commands or anything other than what is lawful.

l: anger, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Anger is withheld by the strong and controlled first by sitting, then by lying down if it does not go away.

l: Hell Fire, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_surrounded_by sins [to make it attractive through desires and vices] Hell Fire is shown to Gabriel and is surrounded by sins, desires, and vices, so that people incline toward it. It is described as the destination of the miserable and as the mother of certain souls.

l: medicine, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_a means of curing pain [created by God for every pain except age] Medicine is recommended because God has created a remedy for every pain except old age.

l: pain, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: has remedy [except when it is age] Every pain is said to have a remedy created by God except the pain of old age, which has no remedy.

l: vanity, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: excludes God [everything is vanity except God] Everything is described as vanity except God. The heart of the old is said to remain young in love for the world and in the length of hope.

l: faith, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Meekness and shame are described as two branches of faith. A believer is said to fight with the sword and tongue, including through verse against infidels.

l: knowledge, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Knowledge suffers from forgetfulness and is lost by sharing it with the unworthy; pursuing it leads toward Paradise, and learned people surpass mere worshippers.

l: Moses, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Moses, elected for prophecy, receives twelve tables and learns his tribe worships a calf; after witnessing it himself, he throws down and breaks the tables.

l: Death, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: is_a dreadful event Death is described as dreadful, and people are told not to wish for it because a person may increase good works or obtain forgiveness through repentance. People should stand when they see a bier, avoid insulting the dead, and not sit on graves or pray facing them.

l: soul, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: The soul leaves the body at death, with the eyes following it. A believer’s soul has a musk scent, is welcomed by merciful angels and faithful souls, and reaches celestial regions; an infidel’s soul reeks and is taken by punishing angels.

l: State after Death, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: The State after Death includes the soul’s reception by the faithful or infidels, punishments for lying, neglecting the Korān, adultery, and usury, and different houses for common believers and martyrs. It also includes the continued existence of souls and scenes shown in the Prophet’s vision.

l: resurrection, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: has signs The resurrection is associated with the trumpet of Isrāfīl and with the condition of people in the futurity. The Prophet says that knowledge of its condition would cause people to weep much and laugh little.

l: Destiny, The Table-Talk of the Prophet Mohammad (Part 2)
s: Destiny includes God’s writing of every created thing, including people’s places in the fire or Paradise, births, deaths, actions, and allowances. Although these matters are appointed, the Prophet says that the happy will do good works and the miserable will do bad works.
